mainTopic: Benefiting from another's property, rebuilding a collapsed two-story house, and the next משנה about collapsed structures
overview: The גמרא opens with רבי יוחנן's claim that in three משניות, רבי יהודה teaches that a person may not benefit from someone else's property. The three are our משנה about the upper story, the dyer who used the wrong color, and the partly paid loan document. The גמרא then pushes back on all three proofs. The rent may be because living in the house blackens the walls. The dyer may lose out because he broke the deal. The loan case may be an אסמכתא, which רבי יהודה holds has no effect. Next, עולא teaches that when the house is rebuilt, the lower owner may only make his walls stronger, and the upper owner may only make his story lighter. If neither owner can afford to rebuild, one ברייתא gives the upper owner nothing in the land, while רבי נתן gives him a third and אחרים a quarter. רבה rules like רבי נתן. A new משנה then brings related cases: a garden on top of a collapsed olive press, a wall or tree that falls into the street, and a wall that falls into a neighbor's garden, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: three places teach that you may not benefit from another's property
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says that in three places רבי יהודה teaches that a person may not benefit from someone else's property. The first place is our own משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רבי יוחנן says: In three places רבי יהודה taught us that a person is forbidden to benefit from his friend's property. One of them is what we learned in our משנה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן introduces a general principle that he says runs through three of רבי יהודה's rulings. He names the first one: our own משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In our משנה, רבי יהודה said the upper-story owner who rebuilt the house and lives in it must pay rent. רבי יוחנן reads this as a broad rule: you may not use another person's property for free, even if the owner loses nothing. He promises two more examples, which are coming next.

keyTerms.meaning: a person is forbidden to benefit

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the whole סוגיא. The rest of the discussion tests whether רבי יהודה really holds this as a general rule.

phrases.english: GEMARA: Rabbi Yochanan says:

phrases.aramaic: בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה מְקוֹמוֹת שָׁנָה לָנוּ רַבִּי יְהוּדָה
phrases.english: In three places Rabbi Yehuda taught us
that a person is forbidden to benefit from his friend's property.
One is what we learned.
phrases.notes: This is our own משנה, where רבי יהודה says the upper-story owner who lives in the rebuilt house must pay rent.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה מְקוֹמוֹת שָׁנָה לָנוּ רַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, a person may not benefit from another's property without paying. Our משנה is the first source for this.

steps.title: Second place: the dyer who used the wrong color
steps.stepSummary: The second source is the dyer who dyed wool the wrong color. רבי יהודה rules that the owner pays the dyer only the lower of his expenses or the added value.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is another place? As we learned: If someone gives wool to a dyer to dye it red, and he dyed it black, or to dye it black, and he dyed it red, רבי מאיר says: the dyer pays the owner the value of his wool. רבי יהודה says: if the added value is more than the expenses, the owner pays the dyer his expenses. If the expenses are more than the added value, he pays him the added value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבי יוחנן's second example: a משנה about a dyer who used the wrong color.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר says the dyer simply pays for the wool and keeps it. רבי יהודה says the owner gets his wool back and pays the dyer whichever amount is lower, his costs or the added value. רבי יוחנן sees in this the same idea: the dyer does not get to keep or profit from someone else's wool.

keyTerms.meaning: the added value (how much the item went up in value)
expenses (the cost of dye and work)

steps.confusionAlert: Watch who pays whom. In רבי מאיר's view, the dyer pays the owner. In רבי יהודה's view, the owner pays the dyer.

phrases.english: What is another? As we learned:
One who gives wool to a dyer
to dye it red for him, and he dyed it black,
black, and he dyed it red,

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: נוֹתֵן לוֹ דְּמֵי צַמְרוֹ.
phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says: He gives him the value of his wool.
phrases.notes: Here the dyer is the one paying, and he keeps the dyed wool.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
If the added value is more than the expenses,
he gives him the expenses,
phrases.notes: Now it is the wool owner paying the dyer.

phrases.english: and if the expenses are more than the added value,
he gives him the added value.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the second of רבי יוחנן's three sources
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's claim that רבי יהודה forbids benefiting from another's property
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about the dyer: רבי יהודה does not let the dyer keep the wool.

steps.title: Third place: the loan document left with a third party
steps.stepSummary: The third source is a debtor who paid part of his debt and left the loan document with a trustee. רבי יהודה says the trustee should not give the document to the lender.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is the other place? As we learned: Someone repaid part of his debt and left his loan document with a third party. He said to him: 'If I do not give you the rest from now until such-and-such a time, give the lender his document.' The time came and he did not pay. רבי יוסי says: the trustee gives it. רבי יהודה says: he does not give it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבי יוחנן's third example: a משנה about a partly-paid loan document left with a trustee.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the trustee gives back the document, the lender can collect the full amount written in it, even though part was already paid. רבי יוסי says the condition stands and the trustee gives it. רבי יהודה says he does not, and רבי יוחנן sees this as the same rule: the lender may not take money that is not truly his.

keyTerms.meaning: deposited with a third party (a trustee)

phrases.english: And what is the other? As we learned:
One who repaid part of his debt
and deposited his document with a third party
and said to him:
"If I do not give you
from now until such-and-such a time,
give him his document."
phrases.notes: "Him" is the lender. With the document back, he could collect the full amount written in it.

phrases.english: The time arrived and he did not pay,
Rabbi Yosei says: He gives it,
Rabbi Yehuda says: He does not give it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the third and last of רבי יוחנן's sources
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's claim about רבי יהודה's general rule
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about the trustee: רבי יהודה says the document is not handed to the lender.

steps.title: Maybe our case is different because the walls get blackened
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why we must read our משנה as a general rule. Perhaps רבי יהודה requires rent only because living in the house blackens its walls.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why? Perhaps רבי יהודה says this only here, because there is blackening.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the first proof. It suggests that רבי יהודה's ruling in our משנה may have a narrower reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן assumed רבי יהודה charges rent even though the house owner loses nothing. The גמרא answers that the owner may in fact lose something: living there blackens the walls and lowers the house's value. If so, our משנה is about causing a loss, not about benefit alone. It no longer proves the broad rule.

keyTerms.meaning: why? (here it is a push-back, not a real question)
he only said it up to here (only in this case)
blackening (of the walls from being lived in)

steps.confusionAlert: "אַמַּאי" looks like a simple question. It is really a challenge to רבי יוחנן's reading.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן says רבי יהודה forbids benefiting from another's property in three משניות. The גמרא starts knocking down the proofs: in our משנה, the blackened walls may be the real reason for the rent.

phrases.english: Why?

phrases.aramaic: דִּלְמָא עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הָכָא,
phrases.english: Perhaps Rabbi Yehuda says this only here,
phrases.notes: "Here" means our משנה, about the house and the upper story.

phrases.english: because there is blackening.
phrases.notes: Living in the house blackens its walls, so the owner does lose something.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמַּאי? דִּלְמָא עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the first of רבי יוחנן's three proofs
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from our משנה (the house and upper story)
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumes the owner suffers no loss. But living in the house blackens the walls, so the rent may be payment for damage, not for benefit alone.

steps.title: The dyer case is about breaking the deal
steps.stepSummary: The dyer ruling may not come from a general rule about benefit. It may come from the rule that whoever changes the agreed terms loses out.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, in the case where he was told to dye the wool red and he dyed it black, רבי יהודה rules that way because the dyer changed what was agreed. And we learned in a משנה: whoever changes the terms ends up with the lower hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the second proof, the dyer case. It gives a different reason for רבי יהודה's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן read רבי יהודה's ruling as coming from the rule against benefiting from another person's property. The גמרא says the real reason may be different: the dyer did not follow instructions, and a person who changes the deal always gets the worse outcome. So this case tells us nothing about benefiting from another person's property.

keyTerms.meaning: One who changes or goes against the agreed terms
His hand is on the bottom. He gets the worse deal.

phrases.english: Or also, the case where he was told to dye it red for him
and he dyed it black
that ruling is because he is changing the deal
and didn't we learn in a משנה:
whoever changes, his hand is on the bottom.
phrases.notes: He ends up with the worse of the possible outcomes, so the dyer collects the lower amount.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי נָמֵי לִצְבּוֹעַ לוֹ אָדוֹם וּצְבָעוֹ שָׁחוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the rejection begun in step 4, now aimed at the second proof
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ruling can be explained as a penalty for changing the agreed terms, not as a rule against benefit

steps.title: The partial-debt case is about an empty promise
steps.stepSummary: The trustee case may not come from a rule about benefit. It may come from the fact that the debtor's deal is an אסמכתא, and רבי יהודה holds that an אסמכתא does not take effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: And in the case of one who repaid part of his debt, the arrangement is also an אסמכתא, and we know that רבי יהודה says an אסמכתא does not acquire.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the third proof, the debtor who paid part of his debt. It gives a different reason for רבי יהודה's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The debtor promised that if he did not pay the rest on time, the lender could take the whole document and collect the full amount again. That is an exaggerated promise he never expected to have to keep, which is called an אסמכתא. רבי יהודה holds an אסמכתא has no legal force, so the trustee does not hand over the document, and the reason has nothing to do with benefit.

keyTerms.meaning: An exaggerated condition a person accepts without truly expecting to fulfill it
We have heard that he holds
It does not acquire. It has no legal effect.

steps.whatToRemember: All three of רבי יוחנן's sources have now been pushed back. The rent case may be about blackening the walls, the dyer case is about changing the deal, and the debt case is about an אסמכתא.

phrases.english: And one who repaid part of his debt
there too, it is an אסמכתא
phrases.notes: His promise to let the lender collect the whole amount if he's late is the kind of promise nobody really means.

phrases.english: and we have heard about רבי יהודה
that he says it does not acquire.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי שֶׁפָּרַע מִקְצָת חוֹבוֹ נָמֵי הָוֵי אַסְמַכְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the rejection by addressing the third and last proof
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ruling can be explained by רבי יהודה's view that an אסמכתא does not take effect

steps.title: The lower owner may change materials only to make the house stronger
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר אדא, quoting עולא, teaches that when the lower-story owner rebuilds, the court lets him switch to stronger materials but not to weaker ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר אדא said in the name of עולא: if the lower owner wants to change how the house is built, we listen to him if he wants to use untrimmed stones, but not hewn stones. We listen to him if he wants beams, but not bricks. We listen to him if he wants to roof it with cedar, but not with sycamore.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching about the collapsed two-story house from our משנה. It asks what changes the lower owner may make when he rebuilds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The upper owner depends on the lower walls to hold up his upper story. So the lower owner may change to materials that are stronger (big untrimmed stones, beams, cedar), because that only helps the upper owner. He may not change to weaker materials (smaller hewn stones, bricks, sycamore).

keyTerms.meaning: The owner of the lower story
Hewn, trimmed stones, which are smaller
We listen to him. The court allows his request.
Sycamore wood, which is weaker than cedar

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read each pair as two separate rules. Each pair is one case: switching to the first material is allowed, and switching from it to the second material is not.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר אַדָּא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּעוּלָּא:
phrases.english: Rav Acha bar Adda said in the name of Ulla:
the lower owner who comes to change the building,
if he wants untrimmed stones, we listen to him;
if he wants hewn stones, we do not listen to him.
If he wants beams, we listen to him.
If he wants bricks, we do not listen to him.
If he wants to roof it with cedars, we listen to him.
If he wants sycamores, we do not listen to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר אַדָּא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּעוּלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the רבי יוחנן discussion and opens a new teaching on rebuilding the collapsed house in our משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The lower owner may change to stronger building materials but not to weaker ones, because the upper story depends on his walls

steps.title: The lower owner and changes to windows and height
steps.stepSummary: עולא's teaching continues for the lower-story owner. He may reduce the number of windows or lower the building, but he may not add windows or raise it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the lower owner wants to have fewer windows, we listen to him. If he wants more windows, we do not listen to him. If he wants to build higher, we do not listen to him. If he wants to build lower, we listen to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the list from Step 7 of what the lower-story owner may change when he rebuilds. These cases are about windows and height.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is the same as in Step 7: the lower owner holds up the upper story, so he may only make changes that keep his walls strong. Fewer windows mean more solid wall, and a lower building is steadier. More windows or a taller building would weaken the support he owes the upper owner.

keyTerms.meaning: We listen to him; the court allows the change
We do not listen to him; the court does not allow the change
To make less (fewer windows, or a lower building)

phrases.english: To reduce the windows: we listen to him.
phrases.notes: We are still talking about the lower-story owner from Step 7.

phrases.english: To increase the windows: we do not listen to him.
To make it higher: we do not listen to him.
To make it lower: we listen to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues עולא's list of allowed and forbidden changes for the lower-story owner.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The lower owner may reduce windows or height. He may not add windows or add height.

steps.title: The upper owner's rule is the reverse: lighter is allowed, heavier is not
steps.stepSummary: For the upper-story owner, the court allows any change that makes his story lighter and forbids any change that makes it heavier.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the upper owner wants to make changes: to build with trimmed stones, we listen to him. To build with large untrimmed stones, we do not listen to him. To build with girders, we do not listen to him. To build with bricks, we listen to him. To roof with cedar, we do not listen to him. To roof with sycamore, we listen to him. To add windows, we listen to him. To have fewer windows, we do not listen to him. To build higher, we do not listen to him. To build lower, we listen to him.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא now gives a parallel list for the upper-story owner. His rule is the opposite of the lower owner's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The upper story rests on the lower owner's walls. So the upper owner may not add weight to them. Lighter materials, more windows, and a lower building are all allowed. Heavier materials, fewer windows, and a taller building are all forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: The owner of the upper story
Thick girders or beams (heavier than bricks)

steps.confusionAlert: Windows work in the opposite direction here. For the lower owner, more windows were forbidden because they weaken his walls. For the upper owner, more windows are allowed because they make his story lighter. The question is always which change protects the other owner.
steps.whyThisMatters: Both lists follow one principle: neither owner may make a change that hurts the other. The lower owner must keep his walls strong, and the upper owner must not make his story heavier.

phrases.english: The upper owner who comes to make changes:
with trimmed stones: we listen to him,
with untrimmed stones: we do not listen to him.
With girders: we do not listen to him,
with bricks: we listen to him.
With cedars: we do not listen to him,
with sycamore: we listen to him.
To increase the windows: we listen to him,
to reduce the windows: we do not listen to him.
To make it higher: we do not listen to him,
to make it lower: we listen to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the matching list for the upper-story owner, using the reverse rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The upper owner may make his story lighter but not heavier.

steps.title: What if neither owner can afford to rebuild?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the law is when neither the upper owner nor the lower owner has money to rebuild.
steps.simpleTranslation: If neither this one nor that one has money, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question: what happens if neither owner can rebuild? This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far, the cases assumed the house would be rebuilt. Now the house cannot be rebuilt, and only the land is left. The question is whether the upper owner still has any share in that land.

keyTerms.meaning: Neither this one nor that one has the means

phrases.aramaic: אֵין לוֹ לָזֶה וְלֹא לָזֶה, מַאי?
phrases.english: If neither this one nor that one has, what is the law?
phrases.notes: "Has" means having the money to rebuild the house.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין לוֹ לָזֶה וְלֹא לָזֶה, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from rebuilding rules to the case where no rebuilding is possible.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who owns the land when neither owner can afford to rebuild the house?

steps.title: A ברייתא: the upper owner has no share in the land
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that if neither owner can rebuild, the upper-story owner has no rights at all in the land.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: if neither this one nor that one has the means, the upper-story owner has nothing in the land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 10 by quoting a ברייתא. The upper-story owner gets nothing from the land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The upper owner only owned living space resting on top of the lower building. He never owned the ground itself. Once the house cannot be rebuilt, his rights end, and the land belongs to the lower owner.

keyTerms.meaning: The owner of the upper story

steps.whatToRemember: While the house stands or is rebuilt, each owner must protect the other's part. This ברייתא says that if the house cannot be rebuilt, the upper owner has no share in the land. The next steps bring other views, and רבה rules like רבי נתן, who gives the upper owner one third.

phrases.english: It was taught in a ברייתא:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין לוֹ לֹא לָזֶה וְלֹא לָזֶה –
phrases.english: If neither this one nor that one has the means,

phrases.aramaic: אֵין לוֹ לְבַעַל עֲלִיָּיה בַּקַּרְקַע כְּלוּם.
phrases.english: the upper-story owner has nothing at all in the land.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא: אֵין לוֹ לֹא לָזֶה וְלֹא לָזֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from Step 10 with a ברייתא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The upper owner has no rights in the land. The land belongs to the lower owner.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: One ברייתא says that if neither owner can rebuild, the upper-story owner has no share in the land; this is later disputed and decided in step 14.

steps.title: רבי נתן gives the upper owner one third of the land
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא quotes רבי נתן: when neither owner can rebuild, the lower owner takes two thirds and the upper owner takes one third.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is taught in a ברייתא: רבי נתן says the lower owner takes two shares and the upper owner takes one third.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different ברייתא. In it, רבי נתן says the upper-story owner does get part of the land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 said the upper owner gets nothing at all in the land. רבי נתן disagrees: the land, or the money from selling it, is split, with two thirds to the lower owner and one third to the upper owner.

phrases.english: It is taught: Rabbi Natan says:
The lower one takes two shares
and the upper one a third.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a competing view to the ברייתא in step 11, which gave the upper owner nothing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Lower owner gets two thirds of the land and the upper owner gets one third.

steps.title: אחרים give the upper owner one quarter
steps.stepSummary: אחרים say the lower owner takes three shares and the upper owner takes one quarter.
steps.simpleTranslation: And אחרים say: the lower owner takes three shares and the upper owner takes one quarter.
steps.whatsHappening: The same ברייתא gives a third opinion. אחרים agree the upper owner gets something, but they give him less.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now there are three views. The first ברייתא gives the upper owner nothing. רבי נתן gives him a third. אחרים give him a quarter, with three quarters going to the lower owner.

phrases.english: And others say:
The lower one takes three shares
and the upper one takes a quarter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A further opinion inside the same ברייתא as רבי נתן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Lower owner gets three quarters of the land and the upper owner gets one quarter.

steps.title: רבה rules like רבי נתן and explains the one-third
steps.stepSummary: רבה says to follow רבי נתן, because he was a judge who understood the law deeply. An upper story lowers a house's value by one third, so the upper owner gets one third.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Follow רבי נתן's view, because he is a judge and goes down to the depth of the law. He holds: how much does an upper story take away from a house's value? One third. So the upper owner gets one third.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה decides the argument in favor of רבי נתן and explains where the number one third comes from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Having someone else's story on top of your house makes the house worth about one third less. That tells us the upper story's share of the property is about one third, so the upper owner gets a third of the land.

keyTerms.meaning: Hold in your hand, meaning follow this view

steps.whatToRemember: The הלכה follows רבי נתן: when neither owner can rebuild, the land is split two thirds to the lower owner and one third to the upper owner. One third is how much an upper story lowers a house's value.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
Hold Rabbi Natan's view in your hand,
phrases.notes: In other words, follow his opinion as the הלכה.

phrases.english: because he is a judge
and goes down to the depth of the law.
He holds:
How much does an upper story take away from a house?
A third.
Therefore he has a third.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides between the views in steps 11 to 13 and explains the reasoning of רבי נתן.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Follow רבי נתן: the upper owner gets one third, because that is how much an upper story lowers the house's value.

steps.title: A garden on top of an olive press that caved in
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: if an olive press built in a rock cave has someone's garden on top and the roof caves in, the garden owner may plant down below until the press owner builds arches to hold the roof up.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Likewise, an olive press built into a rock with a garden on top of it, and the roof broke through. The garden owner may go down and plant below until the press owner builds arches for his olive press.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a case like the two-story house. A garden sits on top of someone else's underground olive press, and the roof collapses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "וכן" (and likewise) ties this to the upper and lower story case. The garden owner keeps his right to farm, so he plants on the fallen ground below. Once the press owner builds supporting arches, the garden goes back on top.

keyTerms.meaning: It caved in or broke through
Arches that hold up a roof

phrases.english: MISHNA:
And likewise, an olive press
that is built in rock
and a garden on top of it,
and it caved in.
The garden owner goes down
and plants below
until he makes arches for his olive press.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן בֵּית הַבַּד שֶׁהוּא בָּנוּי בַּסֶּלַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה with a case similar to the upper and lower story house.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The garden owner may plant below until the press owner builds supporting arches.

steps.title: A wall or tree that falls into the public area
steps.stepSummary: If a wall or tree falls into the public area and causes damage, the owner is exempt. If the court gave him time to remove it, he is exempt if it fell during that time and liable if it fell after the time ran out.
steps.simpleTranslation: A wall or a tree that fell into the public area and caused damage: the owner is exempt from paying. If they gave him time to cut down the tree or knock down the wall and it fell during that time, he is exempt. If it fell after that time, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה moves to a new case: who pays when a wall or tree falls into the street and hurts someone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the fall is an accident, so the owner does not pay. Once the court has given him a deadline to remove it, he has been warned. If it falls after the deadline passes, it is his fault and he pays.

phrases.english: The wall and the tree
that fell into the public area and caused damage:
he is exempt from paying.
If they gave him time
to cut down the tree
or to knock down the wall,
and they fell within the time, he is exempt;
after the time, he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new case in the same משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The owner is exempt unless the court's deadline to remove the wall or tree had already passed.

steps.title: A wall that fell into a neighbor's garden
steps.stepSummary: The משנה begins a case where a wall collapses into a neighbor's garden and the garden owner tells the wall owner to clear his stones.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone's wall was next to his friend's garden and it fell. The garden owner said to him, "Clear away your stones," and the wall owner said to him:
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה is setting up a new case, and it continues past this point. We only hear the start of the conversation here; the wall owner's reply comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The stones now lie in someone else's garden, and the garden owner wants them gone. The question of who must deal with them depends on how the wall owner answers.
